lead: A periodic signal has a line spectrum. An aperiodic signal has no single period, so its spectrum becomes continuous. The Fourier transform is the limit of the exponential Fourier series as the period T₀ goes to infinity. It maps a time signal x(t) to a complex function X(ω) of angular frequency ω in rad/s. Engineers use it to see which frequencies a pulse, a transient or a message occupies, and to compute filtering, modulation and bandwidth. This chapter derives the transform, states when it exists, and builds the standard pairs used everywhere.
prereq: You need: Fourier series, the standard signals (impulse, step, exponential, signum) and limits from first-year calculus.

sections.h3: From Fourier series to Fourier transform

blocks.text: Start with a periodic signal x<sub>T₀</sub>(t), period T₀. Its exponential Fourier series is x<sub>T₀</sub>(t)=Σ c<sub>n</sub> e<sup>jnω₀t</sup>, where ω₀=2π/T₀ rad/s and c<sub>n</sub>=(1/T₀)∫x<sub>T₀</sub>(t)e<sup>−jnω₀t</sup>dt over one period. Define X<sub>n</sub>=c<sub>n</sub>T₀. Then x<sub>T₀</sub>(t)=(1/T₀)Σ X<sub>n</sub> e<sup>jnω₀t</sup>. The line spacing is Δω=ω₀=2π/T₀. As T₀→∞ the signal loses its period, Δω→0, the lines merge, and the sum becomes an integral.
Here x(t) is the time signal (V if voltage); ω is angular frequency in rad/s; j=√−1; X(ω) is the complex spectrum.

Here X(ω) is the spectrum and dω is a small step of angular frequency. The 1/2π comes from the line spacing: the sum (1/T₀)Σ… becomes (1/2π)Σ…Δω, and Δω becomes dω. If you work with f in hertz (ω = 2πf, dω = 2π df), the factor cancels and x(t) = ∫X(f)e<sup>j2πft</sup>df.

The transform exists when x(t) meets the Dirichlet conditions: ∫|x(t)|dt<∞, and only finitely many maxima, minima and finite jumps in any finite interval. X(ω) is then continuous in ω. These conditions are sufficient, not necessary: the constant 1, the step u(t), sgn(t) and cos ω₀t fail them, yet they get transforms that contain impulses (the table below). Some syllabi write X(jω) for the same function.

Use Sa(y)=sin y/y. The rectangular pulse rect(t/τ) equals 1 for |t|<τ/2 and 0 outside. Its transform is τSa(ωτ/2). Some syllabi call this part "Fourier transform of standard signals and periodic signals". The table lists the pairs to memorise. The pulse, the impulse and the two exponentials follow from the defining integral; the constant, the signum, the step and the sinusoids need a limit or duality, and their transforms contain impulses.

blocks.text: A periodic signal is not aperiodic, but its transform is still written as impulse trains: x(t)=Σ c<sub>n</sub> e<sup>jnω₀t</sup> ↔ 2πΣ c<sub>n</sub> δ(ω−nω₀). The impulse train Σ δ(t−nT) ↔ (2π/T)Σ δ(ω−2πn/T). These pairs let Fourier-series results sit inside the transform framework.

A signal is time-limited if x(t)=0 outside a finite interval. It is band-limited if X(ω)=0 for |ω|>B, where B is the bandwidth in rad/s. A nonzero signal cannot be both. If X(ω) is zero above B, the inverse integral runs over finite limits and produces a smooth function that cannot be zero on an interval unless it is zero everywhere. In the other direction, a rectangular pulse of width τ has a sinc spectrum with first zero at ω=2π/τ. Narrower τ gives a wider main lobe. The product τB stays roughly constant. This trade is why a short pulse needs more bandwidth than a long one: a 1 μs pulse has its first spectral zero at ω = 2π×10⁶ rad/s (1 MHz), a 1 ms pulse at 2π×10³ rad/s (1 kHz).

examples.question: For x(t)=e<sup>−2t</sup>u(t), find X(ω). Hence find |X(ω)| at ω=0 and ω=2 rad/s.
steps: Write u(t)=1 for t≥0 and 0 for t<0, so the integral runs from 0 to ∞.
Integrate: X(ω)=[−1/(2+jω)]e<sup>−(2+jω)t</sup> evaluated from t=0 to t=∞.
At t→∞, e<sup>−2t</sup>→0 and |e<sup>−jωt</sup>|=1, so the upper limit gives 0. At t=0 the value is 1. Thus X(ω)=1/(2+jω).
examples.check:
import math
X0 = 1/math.sqrt(4+0**2)
X2 = 1/math.sqrt(4+2**2)
print(X0)
print(round(X2, 3))

examples.question: Find the Fourier transforms of the signum function sgn(t) and the unit step u(t). Check the signum result numerically at ω = 2 rad/s.
steps: sgn(t) is not absolutely integrable (∫|sgn t|dt is infinite), so write it as a limit of a signal that is: sgn(t) = lim<sub>a→0</sub> [e<sup>−at</sup>u(t) − e<sup>at</sup>u(−t)], with a > 0.
Transform the bracket: e<sup>−at</sup>u(t) ↔ 1/(a+jω), and e<sup>at</sup>u(−t) ↔ ∫<sub>−∞</sub><sup>0</sup>e<sup>at</sup>e<sup>−jωt</sup>dt = 1/(a−jω).
Numerical check at ω = 2 rad/s with a = 0.1: −2j(2)/(0.01+4) = −j0.998, already within 0.3% of 2/(j2) = −j1.
Unit step: u(t) = ½ + ½ sgn(t). The constant ½ transforms to ½·2πδ(ω) = πδ(ω), and ½ sgn(t) to ½·2/(jω) = 1/(jω).
So u(t) ↔ πδ(ω) + 1/(jω). The impulse carries the average value ½ of the step; the 1/(jω) part carries the jump.
examples.answer: sgn(t) ↔ 2/(jω), with |2/(jω)| = 1 at ω = 2 rad/s; u(t) ↔ πδ(ω) + 1/(jω).

traps: Forgetting the 1/(2π) factor in the inverse transform. The forward transform has no such factor in this convention.
Mixing f in Hz with ω in rad/s. Use X(ω)=∫x(t)e<sup>−jωt</sup>dt and remember ω=2πf.
Using the wrong denominator for e<sup>−at</sup>u(t). It is 1/(a+jω), not 1/(a−jω), and the lower limit is 0 because of u(t).
Assuming a time-limited pulse is band-limited. A rectangular pulse has sinc tails that never end, so its spectrum is nonzero at arbitrarily high ω.
Treating δ(ω−ω₀) as a finite value. It is a density with unit area; the spectrum of a sinusoid is an impulse, not a tall finite spike.

quiz.q: Write the Fourier transform and its inverse for a continuous-time signal x(t).
Why does an aperiodic signal have a continuous spectrum?
quiz.a: As T₀→∞, the harmonic spacing ω₀=2π/T₀→0. The discrete lines merge into a continuum, so the Fourier series becomes an integral over ω.

quiz.q: Find the Fourier transform of δ(t−3).
For rect(t/2), width 2 centred at 0, find X(ω) and X(0).
quiz.a: Here τ=2, so X(ω)=2Sa(ω). Sa(y)=sin y/y tends to 1 as y→0 (the limit, since 0/0 is undefined), so X(0)=2. Check: X(0)=∫x(t)dt is the pulse area, 2×1=2.

quiz.q: Can a nonzero signal be both time-limited and band-limited? Explain in one line.
quiz.a: No. A band-limited spectrum gives an inverse integral over finite frequencies, which cannot be zero on an interval unless the signal is zero everywhere.

quiz.q: Why is the transform of the constant 1 equal to 2πδ(ω)?
quiz.a: The inverse transform of 2πδ(ω) is (1/2π)∫2πδ(ω)e<sup>jωt</sup>dω=1 for all t.

quiz.q: A pulse is made narrower in time while its height stays fixed. What happens to its magnitude spectrum?
quiz.a: The main lobe widens and the peak value falls. The spectrum spreads over more frequencies, keeping the time-width times bandwidth product roughly constant.

beyond: Not for the exam. Continuous-time Fourier transforms underpin OFDM in 4G and 5G, radar pulse design, and spectral estimation in instrumentation. In research, the same limit idea leads to the Fourier integral theorem and to distributions such as delta functions. Search next for continuous-time Fourier transform, sinc spectrum, band-limited signal, and the Paley-Wiener theorem. Practical software computes the discrete Fourier transform (DFT), which samples this transform.
